creator.name: Moks
creator.expertise: Product designer with 5+ years in healthcare; lifelong reader and book club member; Lagos-based, building alongside cofounder Ayodeji (operations, BD, child-safety background)
creator.background: I'm a product designer by trade — five years in healthcare, a domain that taught me to build for trust, retention, and behavior change. I'm also the reader Flipbook is for: a stack of half-finished books, three abandoned reading apps, and a lifetime of book clubs that started strong and died by chapter three. Flipbook is what I've wanted to exist for a decade, and I finally have the design and product chops to build it. I'm based in Lagos and shipping in the open.

purpose.whoYouHelp: African readers in their 20s–40s — starting with Nigeria, expanding across the continent and diaspora. The person we're building for buys books faster than they finish them, watches BookTok, cannot afford a ₦35,000 hardcover as a habit, and has watched two WhatsApp book clubs stall by Chapter 3. They want to read more, they want to read together, and they want the reading tools that exist in the West priced and curated for the world they actually live in.
purpose.problemYouSolve: Books are inaccessible for most African readers, and reading is lonely once you finally have one. On the access side: a mainstream hardcover in Lagos costs ₦25,000–₦35,000 — a week's discretionary spend. Kindle prices in USD and skews Western in catalog. Local ebook platforms are fragmented and thin on curation. On the community side: reading is a solo act in a culture that's rediscovering it as a shared one. Book clubs form on WhatsApp and die within three weeks because there's no shared surface for the reading itself.
purpose.desiredTransformation: From an inaccessible, lonely act to an affordable, communal one. Before: a reader saves for the one book they can afford, reads it alone in bed, finishes it (maybe), and has nowhere to talk about it. After: the same reader opens Flipbook, rents from a curated catalog of African indie voices and world classics for the price of a coffee, and reads inside a room where their reactions appear next to their friends'. Reading becomes something a Lagos, Accra, or Nairobi reader does weekly — not aspirationally, actually.
purpose.whyYou: Five years of designing healthcare products — a domain where trust, retention, and respect for attention are non-negotiable — mapped exactly onto what a reading + community + payments product needs. I'm not designing for a persona I read about in research: I am the user, I live in the market, and I've abandoned every reading app on the shelf. Being based in Lagos is not incidental — it's the structural advantage. I can sign African indie publishers over coffee that no US or UK reading app can reach.

product.name: Flipbook
product.oneLiner: Flipbook is a book-rental app with community built in — a curated library of African indie voices and world classics, where readers rent affordable books and read them together.
product.howItWorks: A reader downloads Flipbook, browses a curated catalog of public-domain classics and licensed indie books (starting with African authors and small publishers), and rents any title for 4 weeks at prices between ₦500 and ₦4,000 depending on band. They read inside a purpose-built EPUB reader — with in-margin reactions if they're in a community reading the same book. Communities are formed like WhatsApp groups (invite-by-link) around specific books, genres, or interests. A Pro subscription (₦1,550–₦2,500/mo) unlocks unlimited access to public-domain classics, a 15% discount on paid rentals, curated Flipbook Specials, neural-TTS audio narration, and community-creation rights. Independent authors and small publishers license their books to Flipbook for a 70/30 split in their favor; educators can create bounded course-communities to distribute reading lists to their students (an extension, not a separate product).
keyCapabilities: Curated catalog of rentable books — starting with public-domain classics + African indie authors + small African publishers; expanding outward as reader base and supply grow
Tiered rental model — 4 bands (₦500 / ₦1,500 / ₦2,500 / ₦4,000) for a 4-week rental, mapped to book type; not variable per-title, not flat
In-app reading with in-margin community reactions — comments and reactions live next to the paragraph that prompted them, only for readers who share a community and a rental
Communities — book clubs formed like WhatsApp groups, invite-by-link, moderated by their creator, discovering each other through the catalog

Flipbook Pro subscription — three tiers (₦2,500/mo monthly, ₦2,000/mo quarterly, ₦1,550/mo annual); unlocks unlimited Band A, 15% off B/C/D, Specials, audio narration, longer shelves, community creation

Flipbook Specials — a curated set of free-to-Pro titles across three sub-shelves: (1) Flipbook Editions of the classics with editorial care, (2) Flipbook Exclusives with 90-day windows from indie authors, (3) Flipbook Originals (later — commissioned work)
Audio reader — neural-TTS narration pre-generated per book at ingestion, available only to Pro subscribers; author can opt out at signing

Course communities (educator extension) — bounded by academic term, roster-invited, lecturer role can post course materials and see anonymized reading progress; strictly reading-shaped, never LMS-shaped
Author royalty statements + monthly payouts — 70% of every rental to the author, paid monthly via Paystack (NGN) or Wise/PayPal (USD)
Live audio review sessions (fast-follow after MVP launch) — clubs schedule and hold live, Twitter Spaces–style sessions synchronized with the book
Safety-first minor onboarding — neutral date-of-birth gate, adult-provisioned walled garden for under-18s, verifiable-parental-consent staged behind KWS/k-ID
product.marketDifferentiation: Unlike Amazon Kindle (Western catalog, USD pricing, no community), Flipbook is priced in naira and led by African voices. Unlike Goodreads (a graveyard of past reviews) or StoryGraph (a solo tracker), Flipbook is built around the book you're reading right now with the people reading it with you. Unlike Okada Books or Selar (direct sale of individual titles), Flipbook is a rental library — closer to Spotify than to a bookstore — with curation, subscription value, and community layered in. Unlike Fable (book-club-as-content-feed), Flipbook's community is member-led and starts from friends, not from celebrity clubs.
product.magicMoment: A university student in Lagos who couldn't afford the ₦28,000 Damilare Kuku hardcover rents it on Flipbook for ₦1,500. Their sister in Abuja rents it the same day. They form a two-person community. As each of them reads Chapter 4, the other's reactions appear in the margins on their phone — a wry ♥ next to the funniest paragraph, a 'wait, what?' next to the twist. Twelve chapters and two weeks later they've finished the first book they've ever finished together, the author has earned ₦2,100 across the two rentals, and both readers are shopping for what to rent next. This is Flipbook working end-to-end: access, community, and author economics in one moment.

audience.primaryUser: Ada, 27, brand designer in Lagos. Reads on her commute and before bed. Buys one book a month and finishes maybe every third. Has a WhatsApp group with three friends that used to be a book club and is now mostly memes. Spends ₦2,900/mo on Netflix and ₦900/mo on Spotify and considers both essential. Has never paid for a reading subscription because none of them felt made for her. Discovered BookTok during lockdown and follows five Nigerian and diaspora authors on Instagram. Would pay for a well-designed African reading app in a heartbeat.
secondaryUsers: African indie authors and small publishers — the supply side. Self-published authors on Okada Books and Selar, Nigerian and Ghanaian romance writers, Cassava Republic / Farafina / Masobe / Ouida / NLP / Parrésia authors, and the diaspora indie presses. They license their work to Flipbook non-exclusively for a 70/30 rev-share and get access to a reader base and community infrastructure they couldn't build alone.

University lecturers and educators — the third stakeholder surface (extension, not a separate product). Professors distributing course materials, tutorials, and reading lists to their students via bounded course-communities. Strictly reading-shaped: post materials, invite roster, see reading progress. Never assignments, grading, or scheduling — those live in Google Classroom / Canvas / Moodle. Access is the founder-network entry point (Moks's parents are professors); expected to spread lecturer-to-lecturer and campus-to-campus if it holds.

Community moderators — the power users among readers. They create clubs, pick books, drive reading pace. Pro subscription gates the moderator role, so this is also our clearest Pro-conversion pathway.

Guardians and educators running children's book clubs — parents, teachers, and librarians running reading clubs for minors. They are the vetted-adult who provisions children into a specific moderated, private club, gives parental consent, and acts as the responsible moderator. Distinct from the university-educator surface because the core job is walled-garden supervision for under-18s.
audience.currentAlternatives: Direct competitors on the reading side: Amazon Kindle (Western catalog, USD pricing, no community layer), Google Play Books (same story), Kobo (same story), Everand / Scribd (unlimited subscription, weak African catalog). Local ebook platforms: Okada Books, Selar, Bambooks — direct sale of individual titles, no rental model, no community. Reading trackers: Goodreads, StoryGraph — track what you've finished, do nothing for what you're reading right now. Community adjacencies: Discord (dies in three weeks), WhatsApp group chats (die faster), Substack (creators only). Manual alternatives: buying expensive physical hardcovers, pirating PDFs (huge in Lagos), or simply not reading.
audience.frustrations: Access frustration: 'I want to read this book, but ₦35,000 for a hardcover I might not finish is a hard sell.' Cultural-fit frustration: 'The reading apps I've tried are all built for someone in Brooklyn, not Lagos — the catalog, the pricing, the vibe.' Loneliness frustration: 'I finished this incredible book and had no one to text about Chapter 11.' Community-death frustration: 'Every book club I've joined has died by Chapter 3.' Author-side frustration: 'I'm a Nigerian indie author on KU making pennies per page read. I want a platform that actually puts my book in front of readers who'll care.'

revenueStreams: Rental commissions — 30% of every book rental; largest revenue line by volume (rest goes to authors and publishers at 70%)
Flipbook Pro subscription — ₦2,500/mo (monthly), ₦2,000/mo effective (quarterly), ₦1,550/mo effective (annual, 38% commitment discount); highest-margin line
Flipbook Specials licensing (year 1) — flat quarterly fees paid to authors for Specials placement, funded from Pro revenue
Institutional / campus licensing (year 2+) — universities pay per-lecturer or per-department for extended course-community features; explicitly Year-2 revenue, not Year-1

unitEconomics.proDiscount: 15% off Bands B/C/D for Pro subscribers
unitEconomics.rentalBands: A: ₦500 (public-domain); B: ₦1,500 (indie standard); C: ₦2,500 (premium indie / small publisher); D: ₦4,000 (Tier-3 publishers, later)
unitEconomics.monthlyBreakeven: ~1,375 active users + ~95 Pro subscribers at 7% conversion (see docs/model-math.md)

business.initialGoal: First 90 days from July 15, 2026: (1) first paying reader by October 13, 2026, (2) 30 signed African indie authors + small publishers as founding cohort, (3) 500+ public-domain titles ingested and rentable, (4) 5,000+ reader waitlist carrying over from the v1 launch, (5) 2 founding-educator courses live (Moks's parents), (6) v1 (club management) continues shipping in parallel and holds user acquisition warm.
business.sixMonthVision: By March 2027: monthly cash breakeven achieved, ~2,000 active users, 130+ Pro subscribers, catalog of 800+ titles (~200 indie/publisher + 600 PD), 3–5 university course communities live across 2 campuses, first ₦100k+ month in author payouts distributed, first small African publisher signed and integrated.
business.twelveMonthVision: By September 2027: ~5,000 active users, ~400 Pro subscribers (8% conversion), monthly net contribution ₦1.87M (~$1,248), cumulative Year-1 contribution ₦7.17M (~$4,780), catalog of 1,500+ titles, catalog expanding from Nigerian indie into Kenyan, Ghanaian, and South African voices, first small publisher deal fully live, campus surface spreading organically at 2–4 lecturers per new campus.
business.constraints: Two-cofounder team, part-time, bootstrapped from Lagos. **Moks** (designer-founder) owns product direction, vision, design, frontend build, growth, and hands-on supply outreach with individual authors. **Ayodeji** (operations cofounder) runs ops and process, business development, and relationship-building — former Programs Manager at a gaming company with a deep network, strong pitching ability, and hands-on child-safety operations background. In the v2 model, Ayodeji leads small-publisher licensing conversations (Cassava Republic, Farafina, Masobe, etc.), founding-30 author cohort onboarding + statement/payout operations, and campus-surface expansion (warm intros to the next lecturers). No dedicated backend engineer — Convex + AI coding agents (Claude Code) do the heavy lifting. Team-wide time budget: ~50-60 hours/week combined across both cofounders, part-time around day jobs. Software budget realistically ~$50-100/mo through Year 1 (up from ~$15-30/mo pre-pivot — TTS ingestion, hosting, and payment rails are real cost lines now). Nigerian base means every USD-denominated cost line (Convex, OpenAI TTS, ElevenLabs, Vercel, Wise/PayPal payouts) carries currency-depreciation risk. Payment rails require both Paystack (NGN local) and Stripe/Wise (USD diaspora). Hiring plan: first hire (likely backend engineer or community/author-success lead) triggered by first fund raise or sustained monthly cash breakeven, whichever comes first — not before.
business.goToMarket: Three-stream go-to-market. (1) Reader acquisition rides on the v1 community app launch (currently in beta) — every existing waitlist signup and active club is a v2 warm reader. Build-in-public content on X, Instagram, LinkedIn continues as the acquisition engine. (2) Supply-side outreach — 20–40 African indie authors and 2–3 small publishers pitched in weeks 1–8 (see docs/supply/); founding-30 cohort signed by mid-August. (3) Campus pilot — founding-educator cohort begins with Moks's parents' courses; expected to spread lecturer-to-lecturer if it holds; not marketed publicly until signal is proven. Explicit non-goal: no Big-5 publisher outreach in Year 1 — those conversations happen at 10,000+ Pro subscribers with distribution numbers in hand.

productPrinciples: The book is the hero — book content, covers, and reader marks (reactions, highlights) are the visual centerpiece of every screen they appear on. UI chrome stays restrained.

Reading extends. Workflow does not. Flipbook accepts new content types (course notes, reading lists, indie novellas) and new communities (book clubs, courses) freely — as long as the interaction is reading and reacting on the page. Flipbook never builds tools for grading, scheduling, video, or any workflow that could be described as 'learning management.'

Daily return, not session length — Flipbook optimizes for the daily reading habit. Habit mechanics (streaks, goals, contextual reminders, progress celebration) are encouraged when they get someone reading today; mechanics that inflate time-in-app without serving reading (infinite scroll, engagement-bait) are banned. Gamification never shames and never ranks readers publicly against each other.
Curation over recommendation — the catalog grows by editorial choice, not by algorithm. Every book we add is a book we can explain choosing.
Editorial calm over interface noise — generous whitespace, clear hierarchy, type-driven layouts.
Bold accent, restrained system — Vibrant Coral used sparingly and intentionally.
Motion confirms, never distracts — animations are short, purposeful, and tied to user action.

feeling.brandPersonality: Bookish-modern with a cozy-communal undertone. Refined, witty, social, alive — but also warm, intimate, and inviting. Confident that reading is having a moment and acts like it. Confident but not loud, social but not chaotic, beautiful without being precious. Now with a specific cultural anchor: the brand voice comes from Lagos, sounds like a well-read Nigerian friend, and speaks to a global reader from that vantage.
feeling.visualMood: Editorial-modern with strong identity and a three-theme system, sourced from the existing Flipbook Figma design. The brand ships THREE theme modes at MVP: (1) Light — warm/near-white surfaces (Surface Primary #fdfdfd, Warm Ivory #f7f3e3) with Deep Indigo text (#3b3a6d) and Vibrant Coral accents (#ff6b6b/#f83b3b); (2) Flip — the Flipbook-native theme, Deep Indigo surfaces with cream/ivory text and Coral accents, a brand-coded 'candle-lit-reading-nook' aesthetic; (3) Dark — near-black surfaces (#121212) with cream text and Coral accents, high-contrast for low-light reading. Accent highlights: Golden Sand (#e4b363), Muted Plum (#5d3a5a). Typography pairs Raleway (body/headlines) with Inter (UI labels, captions) and Font Awesome 6 Pro for icons. Full structured token set in design-tokens.json.
feeling.toneOfVoice: Warm-witty bookish, with a Lagos accent. Speaks like a literary friend — generous, lightly clever, never cute. Never uses 'platform,' 'leverage,' 'synergy,' 'solution,' 'ecosystem,' 'powered by,' or 'reimagined.' Never ends a sentence with an exclamation point in a notification. Examples — empty catalog: 'Nothing in your library yet. Rent your first book, or wait for a friend to invite you.' Finished a book: 'That's a wrap. Add a thought before it fades?' Rental confirmation: 'It's yours for four weeks. Take your time — the room's here whenever you are.'
feeling.antiPatterns: Don't be Goodreads, don't be Substack, don't be cheap. (Revised Aug 15 2026: the blanket 'don't be Duolingo / never gamify' rule is retired — gamification in service of the daily reading habit is now permitted.) Never feel like a forum from 2008 (no flat threads, no review counts as primary UI, no avatar-and-text grids). Gamify only in service of reading: streaks, goals, and milestones are allowed — warm-toned, personal or club-level, resettable without shame; public leaderboards ranking readers against each other, broken-streak guilt, and status badges remain banned. Reading reminders and re-engagement notifications are allowed — user-controllable, contextual (anchored to the actual book), never shame-framed. Never let book metadata feel like a database. Never let rental checkout feel like a paywall — pricing visible, honest, framed as access. Never feel like an LMS — no grade books, no attendance, no video calls, no assignment submissions. No infinite scroll on the home screen — Flipbook is a place, not a timeline. No algorithmic recommendations as primary discovery. No generic stock photography or AI-generated illustrations. Never crowd a screen. Never use the word 'platform' in user-facing copy.

frontend.rationale: Single codebase for iOS + Android, first-class libraries for offline storage, file handling (PDF/EPUB), and push notifications. Best mobile path for a designer-led two-person team shipping with an AI coding agent.

backend.rationale: Real-time reactivity is exactly what the live in-margin reactions feature needs — no polling, no websocket plumbing. Zero backend boilerplate. Built-in file storage for EPUB assets and cached TTS audio. Best-in-class with Claude Code.

database.rationale: Included with Convex backend. Reactive queries for real-time progress, reactions, and rental status. Document-relational model fits the social/reactive shape of Flipbook.

auth.rationale: Drop-in auth with Apple Sign-In (required for App Store), Google, and phone OTP (important for African markets).

payments.choice: Paystack (NGN local) + RevenueCat (in-app subscriptions) + Wise/PayPal (author payouts) + Stripe (later, USD diaspora)
payments.rationale: Paystack handles Nigerian card rentals and Pro subscriptions with the lowest local fees. RevenueCat manages the App Store / Play Store Pro subscription entitlements globally. Wise / PayPal handle author royalty payouts (USD; Paystack Transfers for NGN payouts). Stripe is deferred to Year 2 for diaspora USD checkout once the Nigerian base is proven. Currency-risk mitigation: bill customers in NGN, hold USD-denominated costs (hosting, TTS) as a hedge line.

audio.choice: OpenAI TTS (general catalog) + ElevenLabs (Specials premium narration)
audio.rationale: Pre-generated at book ingestion, not streamed on-demand. OpenAI TTS at ~$6/book for the general catalog; ElevenLabs at ~$50/book for Specials where quality is a marketing beat. Author opt-out honored per term sheet §4b.
